entries.99fe4272bd0d2e4cd050cd095e44ccce9f01253a: <div sID="gen32662" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Titus.3" sID="Titus.3"/> <div eID="gen32662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32663" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32664" type="x-p"/> Of duties which concern Christians more in common, and the reasons of them, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.1-Titus.3.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. What Titus in teaching should avoid, and how he should deal with a heretic, with some other directions (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.9-Titus.3.14">ver. 9-14</reference>), and salutations in the close, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.15">ver. 15</reference>.
entries.3da28586ccbeec255c26352ab6496614f7ff078e: <div eID="gen32664" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32663" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations to Several Duties; Characteristics of an Unrenewed State; The Import and Origin of Salvation; Regeneration; Justification. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32665" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work, <hi type="super">2</hi> To speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, <hi type="italic">but</hi> gentle, showing all meekness unto all men. 3 For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hating one another. <hi type="super">4</hi> But after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared, 5 Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost; <hi type="super">6</hi> Which he shed on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour; <hi type="super">7</hi> That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life. <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">This is</hi> a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men. <div eID="gen32665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32666" type="x-p"/> Here is the fourth thing in the matter of the epistle. The apostle had directed Titus in reference to the particular and special duties of several sorts of persons; now he bids him exhort to what concerned them more in common, namely, to quietness and submission to rulers, and readiness to do good, and to equitable and gentle behaviour towards all men—things comely and ornamental of religion; he must therefore put them in mind of such things. Ministers are people's remembrancers of their duty. As they are remembrancers for the people to God in prayers (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Isa. lxii. 6</reference>), so are they from God to them in preaching: <hi type="italic">I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.12">2 Pet. i. 12</reference>. Forgetfulness of duty is a common frailty; there is need therefore of reminding and quickening them thereto. Here are the duties themselves, and the reasons of them. <div eID="gen32666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32667" type="x-p"/> I. The duties themselves, which they were to be reminded of. 1. <hi type="italic">Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates.</hi> Magistracy is God's ordinance for the good of all, and therefore must be regarded and submitted to by all; not for wrath and by force only, but willingly and for conscience' sake. <hi type="italic">Principalities,</hi> and <hi type="italic">powers,</hi> and <hi type="italic">magistrates,</hi> that is, all civil rulers, whether supreme and chief or subordinate, in the government under which they live, of whatever form it be; that they be subject to them and obey them in things lawful and honest, and which it belongs to their office to require. The Christian religion was misrepresented by its adversaries as prejudicial to the rights of princes and civil powers, and tending to faction and sedition, and to rebellion against lawful authority; therefore <hi type="italic">to put to silence the ignorance of foolish men,</hi> and stop the mouths of malicious enemies, Christians must be reminded to show themselves examples rather of all due subjection and obedience to the government that is over them. Natural desire of liberty must be guided and bounded by reason and scripture. Spiritual privileges do not make void or weaken, but confirm and strengthen, their obligations to civil duties: "Remind them therefore <hi type="italic">to be subject to principalities and powers and to obey magistrates.</hi>" And, 2. <hi type="italic">To be ready to every good work.</hi> Some refer this to such good works as are required by magistrates and within their sphere: "Whatever tends to good order, and to promote and secure public tranquility and peace, be not backward, but ready, to promote such things." But, though this be included, if not first intended, yet is it not to be hereto restrained. The precept regards doing good in all kinds, and on every occasion that may offer, whether resecting God, ourselves, or our neighbour—what may bring credit to religion in the world. <hi type="italic">Whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report: if there be any virtue, if there be any praise, think on these things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Phil. iv. 8</reference>), to do and follow and further them. Mere harmlessness, or good words and good meanings only, are not enough without good works. <hi type="italic">Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, to visit the fatherless, and the widow in their affliction, and keep unspotted from the world.</hi> "Not only take, but seek, occasion for doing good, keep fitness and readiness that way; put it not off to others, but embrace and lay hold on it thyself, delight and rejoice therein, put all in mind of this." And, 3. <hi type="italic">To speak evil of no man:</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">medena blasphemein,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">to revile,</hi> or <hi type="italic">curse,</hi> or <hi type="italic">blaspheme none:</hi> or (as our translation more generally) <hi type="italic">to speak evil of none,</hi> unjustly and falsely, or unnecessarily, without call, and when it may do hurt but no good to the person himself or any other. If no good can be spoken, rather than speak evil unnecessarily, say nothing. We must never take pleasure in speaking ill of others, nor make the worst of any thing, but the best we can. We must not go up and down as tale-bearers, carrying ill-natured stories, to the prejudice of our neighbour's good name and the destruction of brotherly love. Misrepresentations, or insinuations of bad intentions, or of hypocrisy in what is done, things out of our reach or cognizance, these come within the reach of this prohibition. As this evil is too common, so it is of great malignity. <hi type="italic">If any man seemeth to be religious and bridleth not his tongue, that man's religion is vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.26">Jam. i. 26</reference>. Such loose uncharitable talk is displeasing to God, and hurtful among men. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.9">Prov. xvii. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">He that covereth a transgression seeketh love</hi> (that is, to himself by this tenderness and charity, or rather to the transgressor); <hi type="italic">but he that repeateth a matter</hi> (that blazes and tells the faults of another abroad) <hi type="italic">separateth very friends;</hi> he raises dissensions and alienates his friend from himself, and perhaps from others. This is among the sins to be put off (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.31">Eph. iv. 31</reference>); for, if indulged, it unfits for Christians communion here and the society of the blessed in heaven, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.10">1 Cor. vi. 10</reference>. Remind them therefore to avoid this. And, 4. <hi type="italic">To be no brawlers;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">amachous einai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">no fighters,</hi> either with hand or tongue, no quarrelsome contentious persons, apt to give or return ill and provoking language. A holy contending there is for matters good and important, and in a manner suitable and becoming, not with wrath nor injurious violence. Christian must follow the things that are conducive to peace, and that in a peaceful, not a rough and boisterous and hurtful way, but as becomes the servants of the God of peace and love (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.19">Rom. xii. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath;</hi> this is the Christian's wisdom and duty. <hi type="italic">The glory of a man is to pass over a transgression;</hi> it is the duty of a reasonable, and therefore certainly of a Christian man, whose reason is improved and advanced by religion; such may not, and will not, presently fall foul on one who has offended him, but, like God, will be <hi type="italic">slow to anger, and ready to forgive.</hi> Contention and strife arise from men's lusts, and exorbitant unruly passions, which must be curbed and moderated, not indulged; and Christians need to be reminded of these things, that they do not by a wrathful contentious spirit and behaviour displease and dishonour God and discredit religion, promoting feuds in the places where they live. <hi type="italic">He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.</hi> Wherefore it follows, 5. <hi type="italic">But gentle;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epieikeis,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">equitable and just,</hi> or candid and fair in constructions of things, not taking words or actions in the worst sense; and for peace sometimes yielding somewhat of strict right. And, 6. <hi type="italic">Showing all meekness to all men.</hi> We must be of a mild disposition, and not only have meekness in our hearts, but show it in our speech and conduct. <hi type="italic">All meekness</hi>—meekness in all instances and occasions, not towards friends only, but <hi type="italic">to all men,</hi> though still with wisdom, as James admonishes, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.13">Jam. iii. 13</reference>. "Distinguish the person and the sin; pity the one and hate the other. Distinguish between sin and sin; look not on all alike, there are <hi type="italic">motes and beams.</hi> Distinguish also between sinner and sinner: <hi type="italic">of some have compassion, others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire, thus making a difference,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.22-Jude.1.23">Jude 22, 23</reference>. Mind these things; <hi type="italic">the wisdom that is from above is pure and peaceable, gentle and easy to be entreated.</hi>" Meekness of spirit and demeanour renders religion amiable; it is a commanded imitation of Christ the grand exemplar, and what brings it own reward with it, in the ease and comfort of the disposition itself and the blessings accompanying it. These shall be glad and rejoice, shall be taught and guided in their way, and satisfied with bread, and beautified with salvation. Thus of the duties themselves, which Titus was to put people in mind of: for which, <div eID="gen32667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32668" type="x-p"/> II. He adds the reasons, which are derived <div eID="gen32668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32669" type="x-p"/> 1. From their own past condition. Consideration of men's natural condition is a great means and ground of equity and gentleness, and all meekness, towards those who are yet in such a state. This has a tendency to abate pride and work pity and hope in reference to those who are yet unconverted: "We ourselves also were so and so, corrupt and sinful, therefore we should not be impatient and bitter, hard and severe, towards those who are but as ourselves once were. Should we then have been willing to be contemned, and proudly and rigorously dealt with? No, but treated with gentleness and humanity; and therefore we should now so treat those who are unconverted, according to that rule of equity: <hi type="italic">Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris—What you would not have done to you that do not you to another.</hi>" Their past natural condition is set forth in divers particulars. <hi type="italic">We ourselves also were sometimes,</hi> (1.) <hi type="italic">Foolish;</hi> without true spiritual understanding and knowledge, ignorant of heavenly things. Observe, Those should be most disposed to bear with others' follies who may remember many of their own; those should be meek and gentle, and patient towards others, who once needed and doubtless then expected the same. <hi type="italic">We ourselves also were sometimes foolish.</hi> And, (2.) <hi type="italic">Disobedient;</hi> heady and unpersuadable, resisting the word, and rebellious even against the natural laws of God, and those which human society requires. Well are these set together, <hi type="italic">foolish</hi> and <hi type="italic">obedient.</hi> For what folly like this, to disobey God and his laws, natural or revealed? This is contrary to right reason, and men's true and greatest interests; and what so foolish as to violate and go counter to these? (3.) <hi type="italic">Deceived,</hi> or wandering; namely, out of the ways of truth and holiness. Man in this his degenerate state is of a straying nature, thence compared to a lost sheep; this must be sought and brought back, and guided in the right way, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.176">Ps. cxix. 176</reference>. He is weak, and ready to be imposed upon by the wiles and subtleties of Satan, and of men lying in wait to seduce and mislead. (4.) <hi type="italic">Serving divers lusts and pleasures;</hi> namely, as vassals and slaves under them. Observe, Men deceived are easily entangled and ensnared; they would not serve divers lusts and pleasures as they do, were they not blinded and beguiled into them. See here too what a different notion the word gives of a sensual and fleshly life from what the world generally has of it. Carnal people think they enjoy their pleasures; the word calls it servitude and vassalage: they are very drudges and bond slaves under them; so far are they from freedom and felicity in them that they are captivated by them, and serve them as taskmasters and tyrants. Observe further, It is the misery of the servants of sin that they have many masters, one lust hurrying them one way, and another; pride commands one thing, covetousness another, and often a contrary. What vile slaves are sinners, while they conceit themselves free! the lusts that tempt them promise them liberty, but in yielding they become the servants of corruption; for <hi type="italic">of whom a man is overcome of the same is he brought into bondage.</hi> (5.) <hi type="italic">Living in malice,</hi> one of those lusts that bear rule in them. Malice desires hurt to another and rejoices in it. (6.) <hi type="italic">And envy,</hi> which grudges and repines at another's good, frets at his prosperity and success in any thing: both are roots of bitterness, whence many evils spring: evil thoughts and speeches, tongues <hi type="italic">set on fire of hell,</hi> detracting from and impairing the just and due praises of others. <hi type="italic">Their words are swords,</hi> wherewith they slay the good name and honour of their neighbour. This was the sin of Satan, and of Cain who was of that evil one, and slew his brother; for wherefore slew he him, but of this envy and malice, <hi type="italic">because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous?</hi> These were some of the sins in which we lived in our natural state. And, (7.) <hi type="italic">Hateful,</hi> or odious—deserving to be hated. (8.) <hi type="italic">And hating one another.</hi> Observe, Those that are sinful, living and allowing themselves in sin, are hateful to God and all good men. Their temper and ways are so, though not simply their persons. It is the misery of sinners that thy hate one another, as it is the duty and happiness of saints to love one another. What contentions and quarrels flow from men's corruptions, such as were in the nature of those who by conversion are now good, but in their unconverted state made them ready to run like furious wild beasts one upon another! The consideration of its having been thus with us should moderate our spirits, and dispose us to be more equal and gentle, meek and tenderhearted, towards those who are such. This is the argument from their own past condition here described. And he reasons, <div eID="gen32669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32670" type="x-p"/> 2. From their present state. "We are delivered out of that our miserable condition by no merit nor strength of our own; but only by the mercy and free grace of God, and merit of Christ, and operation of his Spirit. Therefore we have no ground, in respect of ourselves, to condemn those who are yet unconverted, but rather to pity them, and cherish hope concerning them, that they, though in themselves as unworthy and unmeet as we were, yet may obtain mercy, as we have:" and so upon this occasion the apostle again opens the causes of our salvation, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.4-Titus.3.7">v. 4-7</reference>. <div eID="gen32670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32671" type="x-p"/> (1.) We have here the prime author of our salvation—God the Father, therefore termed here <hi type="italic">God our Saviour. All things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2 Cor. v. 18</reference>. All things belonging to the new creation, and recovery of fallen man to life and happiness, of which the apostle is there speaking, all these things are of God the Father, as contriver and beginner of this work. There is an order in acting, as in subsisting. The Father begins, the Son manages, and the Holy Spirit works and perfects all. God (namely, <hi type="italic">the Father</hi>) is a Saviour by Christ, through the Spirit. <reference osisRef="John.3.16">John iii. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">God so loved the world as to give his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him might not perish, but have everlasting life.</hi> He is the Father of Christ, and through him the Father of mercies; all spiritual blessings are by Christ from him, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Eph. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">We joy in God through Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">Rom. v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">And with one mind, and one mouth, glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.15.5">Rom. xv. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen32671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32672" type="x-p"/> (2.) The spring and rise of it—the divine <hi type="italic">philanthropy,</hi> or <hi type="italic">kindness and love of God to man.</hi> By grace we are saved from First to last. This is the ground and motive. God's pity and mercy to man in misery were the first wheel, or rather the Spirit in the wheels, that sets and keeps them all in motion. God is not, cannot be, moved by any thing out of himself. The occasion is in man, namely, his misery and wretchedness. Sin bringing that misery, wrath might have issued out rather than compassion; but God, knowing how to adjust all with his own honour and perfections, would pity and save rather than destroy. He delights in mercy. <hi type="italic">Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.</hi> We read of <hi type="italic">riches of goodness and mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Rom. ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">Eph. ii. 7</reference>. Let us acknowledge this, and give him the glory of it, not turning it to wantonness, but to thankfulness and obedience. <div eID="gen32672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32673" type="x-p"/> (3.) Here is the means, or instrumental cause—the shining out of this love and grace of God in the gospel, <hi type="italic">after it appeared,</hi> that is, in the word. The appearing of love and grace has, through the Spirit, great virtue to soften and change and turn to God, and so is <hi type="italic">the power of God to salvation to every one that believeth.</hi> Thus having asserted God to be the author, his free grace the spring, and the manifestation of this in the gospel the means of salvation, that the honour of all still may be the better secured to him, <div eID="gen32673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32674" type="x-p"/> (4.) False grounds and motives are here removed: <hi type="italic">Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy, he saved us;</hi> not for foreseen works of ours, but his own free grace and mercy alone. Works must be in the saved (where there is room for it), but not among the causes of his salvation; they are the way to the kingdom, not the meriting price of it; all is upon the principle of undeserved favour and mercy from first to last. Election is of grace: we are chosen <hi type="italic">to be</hi> holy, not because it was antecedently seen that we should be so, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Eph. i. 4</reference>. It is the fruit, not the cause, of election: <hi type="italic">God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2 Thess. ii. 13</reference>. So effectual calling, in which election breaks out, and is first seen: <hi type="italic">He hath saved us, and called us with a holy calling; not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2 Tim. i. 9</reference>. We <hi type="italic">are justified freely by grace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Rom. iii. 24</reference>), and sanctified and saved by grace: <hi type="italic">By grace you are saved, through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Eph. ii. 8</reference>. Faith and all saving graces are God's free gift and his work; the beginning, increase, and perfection of them in glory, all are from him. In building men up to be a holy temple unto God, from the foundation to the top-stone, we must cry nothing but <hi type="italic">Grace, grace</hi> unto it. It is <hi type="italic">not of works, lest any man should boast; but of grace, that he who glorieth should glory only in the Lord.</hi> Thus the true cause is shown, and the false removed. <div eID="gen32674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32675" type="x-p"/> (5.) Here is the formal cause of salvation, or that wherein it lies, the beginnings of it at least—in regeneration or spiritual renewing, as it is here called. <hi type="italic">Old things pass away, and all things become new,</hi> in a moral and spiritual, not in a physical and natural, sense. It is the same man, but with other dispositions and habits; evil ones are done away, as to the prevalency of them at present; and all remains of them in due time will be so, when the work shall be perfected in heaven. A new prevailing principle of grace and holiness is wrought, which inclines, and sways, and governs, and makes the man a new man, a new creature, having new thoughts, desires, and affections, a new and holy turn of life and actions; the life of God in man, not only from God in a special manner, but conformed and tending to him. Here is salvation begun, and which will be growing and increasing to perfection; therefore it is said, <hi type="italic">He saved us.</hi> What is so begun, as sure to be perfected in time, is expressed as if it already were so. Let us look to this therefore without delay; we must be initially saved now, by regeneration, if on good ground we would expect complete salvation in heaven. The change then will be but in degree, not in kind. Grace is glory begun, as glory is but grace in its perfection. How few mind this! Most act as if they were afraid to be happy before the time; they would have heaven, they pretend, at last, yet care not for holiness now; that is, they would have the end without the beginning; so absurd are sinners. But without regeneration, that is, the first resurrection, there is no attaining the second glorious one, the resurrection of the just. Here then is formal salvation, in the new divine life wrought by the gospel. <div eID="gen32675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32676" type="x-p"/> (6.) Here is the outward sign and seal thereof in baptism, called therefore <hi type="italic">the washing of regeneration.</hi> The work itself is inward and spiritual; but it is outwardly signified and sealed in this ordinance. Water is of a cleansing and purifying nature, does away the filth of the flesh, and so was apt to signify the doing away of the guilt and defilement of sin by the blood and Spirit of Christ, though that aptness alone, without Christ's institution, would not have been sufficient. This it is that makes it of this signification on God's part, a seal of righteousness by faith, as circumcision was, in the place of which it succeeds; and on ours an engagement to be the Lord's. Thus baptism saves figuratively and sacramentally, where it is rightly used. <hi type="italic">Arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling upon the name of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.22.16">Acts xxii. 16</reference>. So <reference osisRef="Eph.5.26">Eph. v. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">That he might sanctify and cleanse us by the washing of water by the word.</hi> Slight not this outward sign and seal, where it may be had according to Christ's appointment; yet rest not in the outward washing, but look to the <hi type="italic">answer of a good conscience,</hi> without which the external washing will avail nothing. The covenant sealed in baptism binds to duties, as well as exhibits and conveys benefits and privileges; if the former be not minded, in vain are the latter expected. Sever not what God has joined; in both the outer and inner part is baptism complete; as he that was circumcised became debtor to the whole law (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.3">Gal. v. 3</reference>), so is he that is baptized to the gospel, to observe all the commands and ordinances thereof, as Christ appointed. <hi type="italic">Disciple all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost; teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.19-Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 19, 20</reference>. This is the outward sign and seal of salvation, baptism, called here <hi type="italic">the washing of regeneration.</hi> <div eID="gen32676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32677" type="x-p"/> (7.) Here is the principal efficient, namely, the Spirit of God; it is the <hi type="italic">renewing of the Holy Ghost;</hi> not excluding the Father and the Son, who in all works without themselves are concurring; nor the use of means, the word and sacraments, by which the Spirit works; through his operation it is that they have their saving effect. In the economy of our salvation, the applying and effecting part is especially attributed to the Holy Spirit. We are said to be born of the Spirit, to be quickened and sanctified by the Spirit, to be led and guided, strengthened and helped, by the Spirit. Through him we mortify sin, perform duty, walk in God's ways; all the acts and operations of the divine life in us, the works and fruits of righteousness without us, all are through this blessed and Holy Spirit, who is therefore called the Spirit of life, and of grace and holiness; all grace is from him. Earnestly therefore is he to be sought, and greatly to be heeded by us, that we quench not his holy motions, nor resist and oppose him in his workings. <hi type="italic">Res delicatula est Spiritus—The Spirit is a tender thing.</hi> As we act towards him, so may we expect he will to us; if we slight, and resist, and oppose his workings, he will slacken them; if we continue to vex him, he will retire. <hi type="italic">Grieve not therefore the Holy Spirit of God, whereby you are sealed to the day of redemption,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Eph. iv. 30</reference>. The Spirit seals by his renewing and sanctifying, his witnessing and assuring work; he distinguishes and marks out for salvation, and fits for it; it is his work: we could not turn to God by any strength of our own, any more than we can be justified by any righteousness of our own. <div eID="gen32677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32678" type="x-p"/> (8.) Here is the manner of God's communicating this Spirit in the gifts and graces of it; not with a scanty and niggardly hand, but most freely and plentifully: <hi type="italic">Which he shed on us abundantly.</hi> More of the Spirit in its gifts and graces is poured out under the gospel than was under the law, whence it is eminently styled <hi type="italic">the ministration of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.8">2 Cor. iii. 8</reference>. A measure of the Spirit the church has had in all ages, but more in gospel times, since the coming of Christ, than before. <hi type="italic">The law came by Moses, but grace and truth by Jesus Christ;</hi> that is, a more plentiful effusion of grace, fulfilling the promises and prophecies of old. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa. xliv. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thy offspring:</hi> this greatest and best of blessings, an effusion of grace, and of the sanctifying gifts of the Spirit. <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joel ii. 28</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh;</hi> not on Jews only, but Gentiles also. This was to be in gospel times; and accordingly (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.17-Acts.2.18">Acts ii. 17, 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.33">33</reference>), speaking of Christ risen and ascended, <hi type="italic">having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth</hi> (says Peter) <hi type="italic">this that you now see and hear:</hi> and <reference osisRef="Acts.10.44-Acts.10.45">ch. x. 44, 45</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Holy Ghost fell on all those that heart the word,</hi> Gentiles as well as Jews. This indeed was, in a great measure, in the miraculous gifts of the Holy Ghost, but not without his sanctifying graces also accompanying many if not all of them. There was then great abundance of common gifts of illumination, outward calling and profession, and general faith, and of more special gifts of sanctification too, such as faith, and hope, and love, and other graces of the Spirit. Let us get a share in these. What will it signify if much be shed forth and we remain dry? Our condemnation will but be aggravated the more if under such a dispensation of grace we remain void of grace. <hi type="italic">Be filled with the Spirit,</hi> says the apostle; it is duty as well as privilege, because of the means which God in the gospel is ready to bless and make effectual; this is the manner of God's communicating grace and all spiritual blessings under the gospel—<hi type="italic">plentifully;</hi> he is not straitened towards us, but we towards him and in ourselves. <div eID="gen32678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32679" type="x-p"/> (9.) Here is the procuring cause of all, namely, Christ: <hi type="italic">Through Jesus Christ our Saviour.</hi> He it is who purchased the Spirit and his saving gifts and graces. All come through him, and through him as a Saviour, whose undertaking and work it is to bring to grace and glory; he is our righteousness and peace, and our head, from whom we have all spiritual life and influences. <hi type="italic">He is made of God to us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.</hi> Let us praise God for him above all; let us go to the Father by him, and improve him to all sanctifying and saving purposes. Have we grace? Let us thank him with the Father and Spirit for it: <hi type="italic">account all things but loss and dung for the excellency of the knowledge of him,</hi> and grow and increase therein more and more. <div eID="gen32679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32680" type="x-p"/> (10.) Here are the ends why we are brought into this new spiritual condition, namely, justification, and heirship, and hope of eternal life: <hi type="italic">That, being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.</hi> Justification in the gospel sense is the free remission of a sinner, and accepting him as righteous through the righteousness of Christ received by faith. In it there is the removing of guilt that bound to punishment, and the accepting and dealing with the person as one that now is righteous in God's sight. This God does freely as to us, yet through the intervention of Christ's sacrifice and righteousness, laid hold on by faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.20">Rom. iii. 20</reference>, &c.): <hi type="italic">By the deeds of the law shall no flesh be justified;</hi> but through <hi type="italic">the righteousness of God, which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all those that believe,</hi> whence (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.24">v. 24</reference>) we are said to be <hi type="italic">justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins, that he might be just, and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus.</hi> God, in justifying a sinner in the way of the gospel, is gracious to him, and yet just to himself and his law, forgiveness being through a perfect righteousness, and satisfaction made to justice by Christ, who is the propitiation for sin, and not merited by the sinner himself. So it is here: <hi type="italic">Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, that, being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.</hi> It is by grace, as the spring and rise (as was said), though <hi type="italic">through the redemption that is in Christ</hi> as making the way, God's law and justice being thereby satisfied, and by faith applying that redemption. <hi type="italic">By him</hi> (by Christ) <hi type="italic">all that believe are justified from all things from which they could not be justified by the law of Moses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.39">Acts xiii. 39</reference>. Hence the apostle desires <hi type="italic">to be found in him, not having his own righteousness, which was of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith.</hi> Let us not trust therefore in our own righteousness or merit of good works, but in Christ's righteousness alone, received by faith for justification and acceptance with God. Inherent righteousness we must have, and the fruits of it in works of obedience; not however as our justifying righteousness before God, but as fruits of our justification, and evidences of our interest in Christ and qualification for life and happiness, and the very beginning and part of it; but the procuring of all this is by Christ, that, <hi type="italic">being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs.</hi> Observe, Our justification is <hi type="italic">by the grace of God,</hi> and our justification by that grace is necessary in order to our being made <hi type="italic">heirs of eternal life;</hi> without such justification there can be no adoption and sonship, and so no right of inheritance. <reference osisRef="John.1.12">John i. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whoever received him</hi> (namely, Christ), <hi type="italic">to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to those that believed on his name.</hi> Eternal life is set before us in the promise, the Spirit works faith in us and hope of that life, and so are we made heirs of it and have a kind of possession of it even now; faith and hope bring it near, and fill with joy in the well-grounded expectation of it. The meanest believer is a great heir. Though he has not his portion in hand, he has good hope through grace, and may bear up under all difficulties. There is a better state in view. He is waiting for <hi type="italic">an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for him.</hi> How well may such comfort themselves with these words! And now all this gives good reason why we should <hi type="italic">show all meekness to all men,</hi> because we have experienced so much benefit by the kindness and love of God to us, and may hope that they, in God's time, may be partakers of the like grace as we are. And thus of the reasons of equal and gentle, meek and tender behaviour to wards others, from their own bad condition in time past, and the present more happy state into which they are brought, without any merit or deservings of their own, and whereinto by the same grace others may be brought also. <div eID="gen32680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32681" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle, having opened the duties of Christians in common, with the reasons respecting themselves, adds another from their goodness and usefulness to men. Observe, When he has opened the grace of God towards us, he immediately presses the necessity of good works; for we must not expect the benefit of God's mercy, unless we make conscience of our duty (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly</hi> (this is a true Christian doctrine of highest importance, and which ministers must most earnestly and constantly press and inculcate), <hi type="italic">that those who have believed in God</hi> do not think that a bare naked faith will save them; but it must be an operative working faith, bringing forth the fruit of righteousness; they must make it their care <hi type="italic">to maintain good works,</hi> not to do them occasionally only, and when opportunities come in their way, but to seek opportunities for doing them. <hi type="italic">These things are good and profitable unto men:</hi> these <hi type="italic">good works,</hi> say some, or <hi type="italic">the teaching of these things,</hi> rather than idle questions, as follows. These things are good in themselves and the teaching of them useful to mankind, making persons a common good in their places. Note, Ministers, in teaching, must see that they deliver what is sound and good in itself, and profitable to those that hear: all must be to the use of edifying both of persons and societies.
entries.6f336faa425753d089dc583aa9f9e9187d52de53: <div eID="gen32681" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Treatment of Heretics; Apostolic Benediction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32682" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. <hi type="super">10</hi> A man that is a heretic after the first and second admonition reject; <hi type="super">11</hi> Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself. 12 When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus, be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis: for I have determined there to winter. <hi type="super">13</hi> Bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them. <hi type="super">14</hi> And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful. <hi type="super">15</hi> All that are with me salute thee. Greet them that love us in the faith. Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you all. Amen. <div eID="gen32682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32683" type="x-p"/> Here is the fifth and last thing in the matter of the epistle: what Titus should avoid in teaching; how he should deal with a heretic; with some other directions. Observe, <div eID="gen32683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32684" type="x-p"/> I. That the apostle's meaning might be more clear and full, and especially fitted to the time and state of things in Crete, and the many judaizers among them, he tells Titus what, in teaching, he should shun, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">v. 9</reference>. There are needful questions to be discussed and cleared, such as make for improvement in useful knowledge; but idle and foolish enquiries, tending neither to God's glory nor the edification of men, must be shunned. Some may have a show of wisdom, but are vain, as many among the Jewish doctors, as well as of later schoolmen, who abound with questions of no moment or use to faith or practice; avoid these.—<hi type="italic">And genealogies</hi> (of the gods, say some, that the heathen poets made such noise about; or rather those that the Jews were so curious in): some lawful and useful enquiries might be made into these things, to see the fulfilling of the scriptures in some cases, and especially in the descent of Christ the Messiah; but all that served to pomp only, and to feed vanity, in boasting of a long pedigree, and much more such as the Jewish teachers were ready to busy themselves in and trouble their hearers with, even since Christ had come, and that distinction of families and tribes had been taken away, as if they would build again that policy which now is abolished, these Titus must withstand as foolish and vain.—<hi type="italic">And contentious, and strivings about the law.</hi> There were those who were for the Mosaic rites and ceremonies, and would have them continued in the church, though by the gospel and the coming of Christ they were superseded and done away. Titus must give no countenance to these, but avoid and oppose them; <hi type="italic">for they are unprofitable and vain:</hi> this is to be referred to all those <hi type="italic">foolish questions and genealogies,</hi> as well as those <hi type="italic">strivings about the law.</hi> They are so far from instructing and building up in godliness, that they are hindrances of it rather: the Christian religion, and good works, which are to be maintained, will hereby be weakened and prejudiced, the peace of the church disturbed, and the progress of the gospel hindered. Observe, Ministers must not only teach things good and useful, but shun and oppose the contrary, what would corrupt the faith, and hinder godliness and good works; nor should people have itching ears, but love and embrace sound doctrine, which tends most to the use of edifying. <div eID="gen32684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32685" type="x-p"/> II. But because, after all, there will be <hi type="italic">heresies</hi> and <hi type="italic">heretics</hi> in the church, the apostle next directs Titus what to do in such a case, and how to deal with such, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.10">v. 10</reference>. He who forsakes the truth as it is in Christ Jesus, who broaches false doctrines and propagates them to the corrupting of the faith in weighty and momentous points, and breaks the peace of the church about them, after due means used to reclaim him, must be rejected. "Admonish him once and again, that, if possible, he may be brought back, and thou mayest gain thy brother; but, if this will not reduce him, that others be not hurt, cast him out of the communion, and warn all Christians to avoid him."—<hi type="italic">Knowing that he that is such is subverted</hi> (turned off from the foundation) <hi type="italic">and sinneth</hi> grievously, being <hi type="italic">self-condemned.</hi> Those who will not be reclaimed by admonitions, but are obstinate in their sins and errors, <hi type="italic">are subverted and self-condemned;</hi> they inflict that punishment upon themselves which the governors of the church should inflict upon them: they throw themselves out of the church, and throw off its communion, and so are self-condemned. Observe, 1. How great an evil real heresy is, not lightly therefore to be charged upon any, though greatly to be taken heed of by all. Such a one is <hi type="italic">subverted</hi> or perverted—a metaphor from a building so ruined as to render it difficult if not impossible to repair and raise it up again. Real heretics have seldom been recovered to the true faith: not so much defect of judgment, as perverseness of the will, being in the case, through pride, or ambition, or self-willedness, or covetousness, or such like corruption, which therefore must be taken heed of: "Be humble, love the truth and practise it, and damning heresy will be escaped." 2. Pains and patience must be used about those that err most grievously. They are not easily and soon to be given up and cast off, but competent time and means must be tried for their recovery. 3. The church's means even with heretics are persuasive and rational. They must be admonished, instructed, and warned; so much <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">nouthesia</hi></hi> imports. 4. Upon continued obstinacy and irreclaimableness, the church has power, and is obliged, to preserve its own purity, by severing such a corrupt member which discipline may by God's blessing become effectual to reform the offender, or if not it will leave him the more inexcusable in his condemnation. <div eID="gen32685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32686" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle subjoins some further directions, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.12-Titus.3.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. Here are two personal things enjoined:— <div eID="gen32686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32687" type="x-p"/> 1. That Titus should hold himself ready to come to Paul at <hi type="italic">Nicopolis</hi> (a city of Thrace, as is reckoned, on the borders of Macedonia), as soon as <hi type="italic">Artemas</hi> or <hi type="italic">Tychicus</hi> should be sent to Crete, to supply his place, and take care of the churches there when he should leave them. The apostle would not have them in their young and weak state be without one or other of chief sufficiency, to guide and help them. Titus, it seems, was not their ordinary fixed bishop or pastor, but an evangelist, otherwise Paul would not have called him so much from his charge. Of Artemas we read little, but Tychicus is mentioned on many occasions with respect. Paul calls him <hi type="italic">a beloved brother, and faithful minister, and fellow-servant in the Lord:</hi> one fit therefore for the service intimated. When Paul says to Titus, <hi type="italic">Be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis, for I have determined there to winter,</hi> it is plain that the epistle was not written from Nicopolis, as the postscript would have it, for then he would have said, I determined <hi type="italic">here,</hi> not <hi type="italic">there,</hi> to winter. <div eID="gen32687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32688" type="x-p"/> 2. The other personal charge to Titus is that he would bring two of his friends on their journey diligently, and see them furnished, so that nothing should be wanting to them. This was to be done, not as a piece of common civility only, but of Christian piety, out of respect both to them and the work they were sent about, which probably was to preach the gospel, or to be in some way serviceable to the churches. <hi type="italic">Zenas</hi> is styled <hi type="italic">the lawyer,</hi> whether in reference to the Roman or the Mosaic law, as having some time been his profession, is doubtful. <hi type="italic">Apollos</hi> was an eminent and faithful minister. Accompanying such persons part of their way, and accommodating them for their work and journeys, was a pious and needful service; and to further this, and lay in for it, what the apostle had before exhorted Titus to teach (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.8">v. 8</reference>) he repeats here: <hi type="italic">Let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.3.14">v. 14</reference>. Let Christians, those who have believed in God, learn to <hi type="italic">maintain good works,</hi> especially such as these, supporting ministers in their work of preaching and spreading the gospel, hereby becoming <hi type="italic">fellow-helpers to the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.5-3John.1.8">3 John 5-8</reference>. <hi type="italic">That they be not unfruitful.</hi> Christianity is not a fruitless profession; the professors of it must be <hi type="italic">filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are by Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.</hi> It is not enough that they be harmless, but they must be profitable, doing good, as well as eschewing evil.—"<hi type="italic">Let ours</hi> set up and maintain some honest labour and employment, to provide for themselves and their families, that they be not unprofitable burdens on the earth;" so some understand it. Let them not think that Christianity gives them a writ of ease; no, it lays an obligation upon them to seek some honest work and calling, and therein <hi type="italic">to abide with God.</hi> This is of good report, will credit religion and be good to mankind; they will not be unprofitable members of the body, not burdensome and chargeable to others, but enabled to be helpful to those in want. <hi type="italic">To maintain good works for necessary uses;</hi> not living like drones on the labours of others, but themselves fruitful to the common benefit. <div eID="gen32688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32689" type="x-p"/> IV. The apostle concludes with salutations and benedictions, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">v. 5</reference>. Though perhaps not personally known (some of them at least), yet all by Paul testify their love and good wishes to Titus, owning him thereby in his work, and stimulating him to go on therein. Great comfort and encouragement it is to have the heart and prayers of other Christians with and for us. <hi type="italic">Greet those that love us in the faith,</hi> or <hi type="italic">for the faith,</hi> who are our loving fellow-christians. Holiness, or the image of God in any, is the great endearing thing that gives strength to all other bonds, and is itself the best. <hi type="italic">Grace be with you all. Amen.</hi> This is the closing benediction, not to Titus alone, but to all the faithful with him, which shows that though the epistle bears the single name of Titus in the inscription, yet it was for the use of the churches there, and they were in the eye, and upon the heart, of the apostle, in the writing of it. "<hi type="italic">Grace be with you all,</hi> the love and favour of God, with the fruits and effects thereof, according to need, spiritual ones especially, and the increase and feeling of them more and more in your souls." This is the apostle's wish and prayer, showing his affection to them, his desire of their good, and a means of obtaining for them, and bringing down upon them, the thing requested. Observe, Grace is the chief thing to be wished and begged for, with respect to ourselves or others; it is, summarily, all good. <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> shuts up the prayer, expressing desire and hope, that so it may, and so it shall be.  <chapter eID="Titus.3"/> <div eID="gen32689" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen32584" osisID="Titus" type="book"/>

entries.e34749fc7ac6f8f9bae81e612b957992a9ba6c6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18282"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Titus.3.1-Titus.3.15">Tit 3:1-15</reference>. What Titus Is to Teach Concerning Christians' Behavior towards the World: How He Is to Treat Heretics: When and Where He Is to Meet Paul. Salutation. Conclusion.</title> <div sID="gen38001" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18282"/><hi type="bold">1. Put them in mind--</hi>as they are in danger of forgetting their duty, though knowing it. The opposition of Christianity to heathenism, and the natural disposition to rebellion of the Jews under the Roman empire (of whom many lived in Crete), might lead many to forget practically what was a recognized Christian principle in theory, submission to the powers that be. Diodorus Siculus mentions the tendency of the Cretans to riotous insubordination.<div eID="gen38001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be subject--</hi>"willingly" (so the Greek).<div eID="gen38002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">principalities ... powers--</hi>Greek, "magistracies ... authorities."<div eID="gen38003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to obey--</hi>the commands of "magistrates"; not necessarily implying spontaneous obedience. Willing obedience is implied in "ready to every good work." Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.13.3">Ro 13:3</reference>, as showing that obedience to the magistracy would tend to good works, since the magistrate's aim generally is to favor the good and punish the bad. Contrast "disobedient" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.3">Tit 3:3</reference>). <div eID="gen38004" type="x-p"/>
entries.28e674b0eb6310c5e327151fb7a26844bea22419: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18283"/><div sID="gen38005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18283"/><hi type="bold">2. To speak evil of no man--</hi>especially, not of "dignities" and magistrates.<div eID="gen38005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no brawlers--</hi>"not quarrelsome," not attacking others.<div eID="gen38006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gentle--</hi>towards those who attack us. Yielding, considerate, not urging one's rights to the uttermost, but forbearing and kindly (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Php 4:5</reference>). Very different from the innate greediness and spirit of aggression towards others which characterized the Cretans.<div eID="gen38007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">showing--</hi>in acts.<div eID="gen38008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>all possible.<div eID="gen38009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meekness--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.1">2Co 10:1</reference>); the opposite of passionate severity.<div eID="gen38010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto all men--</hi>The duty of Christian conduct towards all men is the proper consequence of the universality of God's grace to all men, so often set forth in the pastoral Epistles. <div eID="gen38011" type="x-p"/>
entries.c614d108fec29f6f0c0c1f300e019d5319c2385e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18284"/><div sID="gen38012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18284"/><hi type="bold">3. For--</hi>Our own past sins should lead us to be lenient towards those of others. "Despise none, for such wast thou also." As the penitent thief said to his fellow thief, "Dost thou not fear God ... seeing that thou art in the same condemnation."<div eID="gen38012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we--</hi>Christians.<div eID="gen38013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were--</hi>Contrast <reference osisRef="Titus.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>, "But when," that is, now: a favorite contrast in Paul's writing, that between our past state by nature, and our present state of deliverance from it by grace. As God treated us, we ought to treat our neighbor.<div eID="gen38014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sometimes--</hi>once.<div eID="gen38015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foolish--</hi>wanting right reason in our course of living. Irrational. The exact picture of human life without grace. Grace is the sole remedy for foolishness.<div eID="gen38016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">disobedient--</hi>to God.<div eID="gen38017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceived--</hi>led astray. The same Greek, "out of the way" (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.2">He 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen38018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">serving--</hi>Greek, "in bondage to," serving as slaves."<div eID="gen38019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divers--</hi>The cloyed appetite craves constant variety.<div eID="gen38020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasures--</hi>of the flesh.<div eID="gen38021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">malice--</hi>malignity.<div eID="gen38022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hateful ... hating--</hi>correlatives. Provoking the hatred of others by their detestable character and conduct, and in turn hating them. <div eID="gen38023" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b48d0000e89a40815baef43d53d59f847ef2f0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18285"/><div sID="gen38024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18285"/>4. To show how little reason the Cretan Christians had to be proud of themselves, and despise others not Christians (see on <reference osisRef="Titus.3.2">Tit 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.3">3</reference>). It is to the "kindness and love of God," not to their own merits, that they owe salvation.<div eID="gen38024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kindness--</hi>Greek, "goodness," "benignity," which manifests His grace.<div eID="gen38025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love ... toward man--</hi>teaching us to have such "love (benevolence) toward man" (Greek, "philanthropy"), "showing all meekness unto all men" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.2">Tit 3:2</reference>), even as God had "toward man" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>); opposed to the "hateful and hating" characteristics of unrenewed men, whose wretchedness moved God's benevolent kindness.<div eID="gen38026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God our Saviour--</hi>Greek, "of our Saviour God," namely, the Father (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">Tit 1:3</reference>), who "saved us" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>) "through Jesus Christ our Saviour" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.6">Tit 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen38027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appeared--</hi>Greek, "was made to appear"; was manifested. <div eID="gen38028" type="x-p"/>
entries.78e0605ac7d8f316a5c7b1d373cff77c3d98b6c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18286"/><div sID="gen38029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18286"/><hi type="bold">5. Not by--</hi>Greek, "Out of"; "not as a result springing from works," &c.<div eID="gen38029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of righteousness--</hi>Greek, "in righteousness," that is, wrought "in a state of righteousness": as "deeds ... wrought in God." There was an utter absence in us of the element ("righteousness") in which alone righteous works could be done, and so necessarily an absence of the works. "We neither did works of righteousness, nor were saved in consequence of them; but His goodness did the whole" [Theophylact].<div eID="gen38030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we--</hi>emphatically opposed to "His."<div eID="gen38031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercy--</hi>the prompting cause of our salvation individually: "In pursuance of His mercy." His kindness and love to man were manifested in redemption once for all wrought by Him for mankind generally; His mercy is the prompting cause for our individual realization of it. Faith is presupposed as the instrument of our being "saved"; our being so, then, is spoken of as an accomplished fact. Faith is not mentioned, but only God's part. as Paul's object here is not to describe man's new state, but the saving agency of God in bringing about that state, independent of all merit on the man's part (see on <reference osisRef="Titus.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen38032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Greek, "through"; by means of.<div eID="gen38033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the washing--</hi>rather, "the laver," that is, the baptismal font.<div eID="gen38034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of regeneration--</hi>designed to be the visible instrument of regeneration. "The apostles are wont to draw an argument from the sacraments to prove the thing therein signified, because it ought to be a recognized principle among the godly, that God does not mark us with empty signs, but by His power inwardly makes good what He demonstrates by the outward sign. Wherefore baptism is congruously and truly called the laver of regeneration. We must connect the sign and thing signified, so as not to make the sign empty and ineffectual; and yet not, for the sake of honoring the sign, to detract from the Holy Spirit what is peculiarly His" [Calvin], (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>). Adult candidates for baptism are presupposed to have had repentance and faith (for Paul often assumes in faith and charity that those addressed are what they profess to be, though in fact some of them were not so, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>), in which case baptism would be the visible "laver or regeneration" to them, "faith being thereby confirmed, and grace increased, by virtue of prayer to God" [Article XXVII, Church of England]. Infants are charitably presumed to have received a grace in connection with their Christian descent, in answer to the believing prayers of their parents or guardians presenting them for baptism, which grace is visibly sealed and increased by baptism, "the laver of regeneration." They are presumed to be then regenerated, until years of developed consciousness prove whether they have been actually so or not. "Born of (from) water and (no 'of' in Greek) the Spirit." The Word is the remote and anterior instrument of the new birth; Baptism, the proximate instrument. The Word, the instrument to the individual; Baptism, in relation to the Society of Christians. The laver of cleansing stood outside the door of the tabernacle, wherein the priest had to wash before entering the Holy Place; so we must wash in the laver of regeneration before we can enter the Church, whose members are "a royal priesthood." "Baptism by the Spirit" (whereof water baptism is the designed accompanying seal) makes the difference between Christian baptism and that of John. As Paul presupposes the outward Church is the visible community of the redeemed, so he speaks of baptism on the supposition that it answers to its idea; that all that is inward belonging to its completeness accompanied the outward. Hence he here asserts of outward baptism whatever is involved in the believing appropriation of the divine facts which it symbolizes, whatever is realized when baptism fully corresponds to its original design. So <reference osisRef="Gal.3.27">Ga 3:27</reference>; language holding good only of those in whom the inward living communion and outward baptism coalesce. "Saved us" applies fully to those truly regenerate alone; in a general sense it may include many who, though put within reach of salvation, shall not finally be saved. "Regeneration" occurs only once more in New Testament, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>, that is, the new birth of the heaven and earth at Christ's second coming to renew all material things, the human body included, when the creature, now travailing in labor-throes to the birth, shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. Regeneration, which now begins in the believer's soul, shall then be extended to his body, and thence to all creation.<div eID="gen38035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and renewing--</hi>not "the laver ('washing') of renewing," but "and BY the renewing," &c., following "saved us." To make "renewing of the Holy Ghost" follow "the laver" would destroy the balance of the clauses of the sentence, and would make baptism the seal, not only of regeneration, but also of the subsequent process of progressive sanctification ("renewing of the Holy Ghost"). Regeneration is a thing once for all done; renewing is a process daily proceeding. As "the washing," or "laver," is connected with "regeneration," so the "renewing of the Holy Ghost" is connected with "shed on us abundantly" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.6">Tit 3:6</reference>). <div eID="gen38036" type="x-p"/>
entries.61e7ee04f701db427b4ffa4e57e76d0218ea0aae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18287"/><div sID="gen38037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18287"/><hi type="bold">6. Which--</hi>the Holy Ghost.<div eID="gen38037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shed--</hi>Greek, "poured out"; not only on the Church in general at Pentecost, but also "on us" individually. This pouring out of the Spirit comprehends the grace received before, in, and subsequently to, baptism.<div eID="gen38038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundantly--</hi>Greek, "richly" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen38039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through Jesus Christ--</hi>the channel and Mediator of the gift of the Holy Ghost.<div eID="gen38040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our Saviour--</hi>immediately; as the Father is mediately "our Saviour." The Father is the author of our salvation and saves us by Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen38041" type="x-p"/>
entries.65e0d8386fab1d9f18d69b7f30ceb9501a16cdcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18288"/><div sID="gen38042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18288"/><hi type="bold">7. That, &c.--</hi>the purpose which He aimed at in having "saved us" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>), namely, "That being (having been) justified (accounted righteous through faith at our 'regeneration,' and made righteous by the daily 'renewing of the Holy Ghost') by His grace (as opposed to works, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>) we should be made heirs."<div eID="gen38042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his grace--</hi>Greek, "the grace of the former," that is, God (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">Ro 5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen38043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heirs--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.3.29">Ga 3:29</reference>).<div eID="gen38044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the hope of eternal life--</hi><reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">Tit 1:2</reference>, and also the position of the Greek words, confirm English Version, that is, agreeably to the hope of eternal life; the eternal inheritance fully satisfying the hope. Bengel and Ellicott explain it, "heirs of eternal life, in the way of hope," that is, not yet in actual possession. Such a blessed hope, which once was not possessed, will lead a Christian to practice holiness and meekness toward others, the lesson especially needed by the Cretans. <div eID="gen38045" type="x-p"/>
entries.30b57b9c3d9d2dd43a0525a62ccab08a3cdc1a80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18289"/><div sID="gen38046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18289"/>8. Greek, "faithful is the saying." A formula peculiar to the Pastoral Epistles. Here "the saying" is the statement (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.4-Titus.3.7">Tit 3:4-7</reference>) as to the gratuitousness of God's gift of salvation. Answering to the "Amen."<div eID="gen38046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these things, &c.--</hi>Greek, "concerning these things (the truths dwelt on, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.4-Titus.3.7">Tit 3:4-7</reference>; not as English Version, what follow), I will that thou affirm (insist) strongly and persistently, in order that they who have believed God (the Greek for 'believed in God' is different, <reference osisRef="John.14.1">Joh 14:1</reference>. 'They who have learnt to credit God' in what He saith) may be careful ('Solicitously sedulous'; diligence is necessary) to maintain (literally, 'to set before themselves so as to sustain') good works." No longer applying their care to "unprofitable" and unpractical speculations (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen38047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">These things--</hi>These results of doctrine ("good works") are "good and profitable unto men," whereas no such practical results flow from "foolish questions." So Grotius and Wiesinger. But Alford, to avoid the tautology, "these (good works) are good unto men," explains, "these truths" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.4-Titus.3.7">Tit 3:4-7</reference>). <div eID="gen38048" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ae0b08e041ffe01cda047b4dd140c68d5822389: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18290"/><div sID="gen38049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18290"/><hi type="bold">9. avoid--</hi>stand aloof from. Same Greek, as in <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Ti 2:16</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Ti 2:16</reference>.<div eID="gen38049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foolish--</hi>Greek, "insipid"; producing no moral fruit. "Vain talkers."<div eID="gen38050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">genealogies--</hi>akin to the "fables" (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>). Not so much direct heresy as yet is here referred to, as profitless discussions about genealogies of aeons, &c., which ultimately led to Gnosticism. Synagogue discourses were termed daraschoth, that is, "discussions." Compare "disputer of this world (Greek, 'dispensation')."<div eID="gen38051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strivings about the law--</hi>about the authority of the "commandments of men," which they sought to confirm by the law (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.7">1Ti 1:7</reference>), and about the mystical meaning of the various parts of the law in connection with the "genealogies." <div eID="gen38052" type="x-p"/>
entries.a95ca37fbecd4ffe198b8b801dc51eec3d2eca4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18291"/><div sID="gen38053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18291"/><hi type="bold">10. heretic--</hi>Greek "heresy," originally meant a division resulting from individual self-will; the individual doing and teaching what he chose, independent of the teaching and practice of the Church. In course of time it came to mean definitely "heresy" in the modern sense; and in the later Epistles it has almost assumed this meaning. The heretics of Crete, when Titus was there, were in doctrine followers of their own self-willed "questions" reprobated in <reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>, and immoral in practice.<div eID="gen38053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reject--</hi>decline, avoid; not formal excommunication, but, "have nothing more to do with him," either in admonition or intercourse. <div eID="gen38054" type="x-p"/>
entries.553ca11ea77a33718fd5879f12706eedb1562b06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18292"/><div sID="gen38055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18292"/><hi type="bold">11. is ... subverted--</hi>"is become perverse."<div eID="gen38055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">condemned of himself--</hi>He cannot say, no one told him better: continuing the same after frequent admonition, he is self-condemned. "He sinneth" wilfully against knowledge. <div eID="gen38056" type="x-p"/>
entries.b49eeef392e838680fc0d52becb660d94e50bcc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18293"/><div sID="gen38057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18293"/><hi type="bold">12. When I shall send--</hi>have sent.<div eID="gen38057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Artemas or Tychicus--</hi>to supply thy place in Crete. Artemas is said to have been subsequently bishop of Lystra. Tychicus was sent twice by Paul from Rome to Lesser Asia in his first imprisonment (which shows how well qualified he was to become Titus' successor in Crete); <reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Ep 6:21</reference>; and in his second, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:12</reference>. Tradition makes him subsequently bishop of Chalcedon, in Bithynia.<div eID="gen38058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Nicopolis--</hi>"the city of victory," called so from the battle of Actium, in Epirus. This Epistle was probably written from Corinth in the autumn. Paul purposed a journey through Ætolia and Acarnania, into Epirus, and there "to winter." See my Introduction to the Pastoral Epistles. <div eID="gen38059" type="x-p"/>
entries.91d408571098ffdc796e07fe36d970c67432851f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18294"/><div sID="gen38060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18294"/><hi type="bold">13. Bring ... on their journey--</hi>Enable them to proceed forward by supplying necessaries for their journey.<div eID="gen38060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zenas--</hi>the contracted form of Zenodorus.<div eID="gen38061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lawyer--</hi>a Jewish "scribe," who, when converted, still retained the title from his former occupation. A civil lawyer.<div eID="gen38062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Apollos--</hi>with Zenas, probably the bearers of this Epistle. In <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.12">1Co 16:12</reference>, Apollos is mentioned as purposing to visit Corinth; his now being at Corinth (on the theory of Paul being at Corinth when he wrote) accords with this purpose. Crete would be on his way either to Palestine or his native place, Alexandria. Paul and Apollos thus appear in beautiful harmony in that very city where their names had been formerly the watchword of unchristian party work. It was to avoid this party rivalry that Apollos formerly was unwilling to visit Corinth though Paul desired him. Hippolytus mentions Zenas as one of the Seventy, and afterwards bishop of Diospolis. <div eID="gen38063" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3cb5dfe1f5c376920edda18cbdeaeb914e85a58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18295"/><div sID="gen38064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18295"/><hi type="bold">14. And ... also--</hi>Greek, "But ... also." Not only thou, but let others also of "our" fellow believers (or "whom we have gained over at Crete") with thee.<div eID="gen38064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for necessary uses--</hi>to supply the necessary wants of Christian missionaries and brethren, according as they stand in need in their journeys for the Lord's cause. Compare <reference osisRef="Titus.1.8">Tit 1:8</reference>, "a lover of hospitality." <div eID="gen38065" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4718dacd062709354bae2bc603fbe448e167e6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18296"/><div sID="gen38066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18296"/><hi type="bold">15. Greet--</hi>"Salute them that love us in the faith." All at Crete had not this love rooted in faith, the true bond of fellowship. A salutation peculiar to this Epistle, such as no forger would have used.<div eID="gen38066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Grace--</hi>Greek, "The grace," namely, of God.<div eID="gen38067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with you all--</hi>not that the Epistle is addressed to all the Cretan Christians, but Titus would naturally impart it to his flock. <chapter eID="Titus.3"/><div eID="gen38068" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen37860" osisID="Titus" type="book"/>

entries.6129ef20e809e18f0ce81b2d6ac2daf6a4ce5f26: <div eID="gen52424" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen52425" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52426" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52426" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52425" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52427" type="x-p"/> The necessity of obedience to the civil powers, and of meek and gentle deportment towards all men, is to be diligently enforced, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.1">Tit 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.2">Tit 3:2</reference>. The wretched state of man, previously to the advent of Christ, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.3">Tit 3:3</reference>. The wonderful change which the grace of God makes, and the means which it uses to bring men to glory, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.4-Tit.3.7">Tit 3:4-7</reference>. The necessity of a holy life, and of avoiding things which produce strifes and contentions, and are unprofitable and vain, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.8">Tit 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>. How to deal with those who are heretics, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.10">Tit 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.11">Tit 3:11</reference>. St. Paul directs Titus to meet him at Nicopolis, and to bring Zenas and Apollos with him, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>; 13. Concluding directions and salutations, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.14">Tit 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.15">Tit 3:15</reference>. <div eID="gen52427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52428" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen52428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52429" type="x-p"/> Put them in mind to be subject to principalities, etc. - By principalities, αρχαις, we are to understand the Roman emperors, or the supreme civil powers in any place. <div eID="gen52429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52430" type="x-p"/> By powers, εξουσιαις, we are to understand the deputies of the emperors, such as proconsuls, etc., and all such as are in authority - under the supreme powers wherever we dwell. See the doctrine of obedience to the civil powers discussed at large in the notes on <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1-Rom.13.7">Rom 13:1-7</reference>. <div eID="gen52430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52431" type="x-p"/> This doctrine of obedience to the civil powers was highly necessary for the Cretans, who were reputed a people exceedingly jealous of their civil privileges, and ready to run into a state of insurrection when they suspected any attempt on the part of their rulers to infringe their liberties. Suidas, under the word ανεσειον, they stirred up, gives the following fragment: Οἱ δε Κρητες, φοβουμενοι μη τι τιμωριας τυχωσιν, ανεσειον τα πληθη, παρακαλουντες την εξ αιωνος παραδεδομενην ελευθεριαν διαφυλαττειν.
